The file name is fine; the problem is argument order. `--json` is a list-taking flag, so it keeps consuming the words after it as its value. In your command it took both `results.json` and `./plugins/notes`, and `./plugins/notes` does not end in .json, which is exactly what the error complains about. Put the target first and the flags after it:

```bash
claude plugin eval ./plugins/notes --json results.json
```

With the path in front, `--json` receives exactly one word, `results.json`, and the extension check passes. You don't need to quote anything or rename the file. The same rule applies to `--tag` and `--allow-tools`: they also take the words after them, so keep them after the target too.

Order is the culprit. `--json` takes the words that follow it as values, so your plugin path was swallowed into it and failed the .json check. Lead with the target:

```bash
claude plugin eval ./plugins/notes --trust-plugin --json results.json
```

Two things to keep in mind. `--tag` and `--allow-tools` behave the same way, so if you add either one, it also goes after the target. And `--trust-plugin` only matters when nothing can answer the first-run trust prompt, such as a CI job; at an interactive terminal you can leave it out.
